summaryTr: Chief Justice Jo Hee-dae criticized the violation of judicial independence.
The statement revealed the reality of the judiciary's political independence being threatened.

summaryTr: The 'Committee of Light,' affiliated with President Lee Jae-myung, was launched to commemorate resistance against martial law.

editorial.titleTr: Opinion: How Did a Satellite Party Alumna Like Yong Hye-in Become an Opposition Lawmaker?
summaryTr: Rep. Yong Hye-in of the Basic Income Party insisted on maintaining her parliamentary seat while serving as minister.
The argument is that proportional representation seats carry party representation, so the resignation convention is not about 'dividing up positions.'
The question is raised whether a politician who benefited from loopholes as a product of a satellite party is fit to be minister.
editorial.bodyTr:
Rep. Yong Hye-in of the Basic Income Party, nominated as minister of gender equality and family, refuted criticism directed at her yesterday and stated her intention to maintain both her ministerial position and her National Assembly seat. She argued that concurrent service as a lawmaker and government minister is permitted by law, and questioned whether the convention of having only proportional representation lawmakers resign upon becoming minister—unlike constituency representatives—amounts to politicians dividing up positions among themselves. However, this is merely sophistry that distorts the fundamental principles of representative democracy and the essence of the proportional representation system.

Constituency representatives and proportional representation lawmakers have different representative mandates. Constituency representatives are elected by local voters who cast ballots based on the individual candidate's character and platform. When a constituency representative resigns due to ministerial duties or other reasons, their constituent district loses its representative voice and must hold a by-election. Proportional representation lawmakers, by contrast, have their seats allocated according to the vote share earned by their party, not by individual candidates. Voters cast ballots based on the party's policies, values, and nomination order. Therefore, if a proportional representative resigns, the successor on the party list assumes the seat without creating a vacancy.

Rep. Yong's refusal to resign from her Assembly seat is merely a calculation to maintain her Basic Income Party's status as a parliamentary party. This is because her proportional seat would otherwise transfer to a Democratic Party member. Furthermore, Rep. Yong characterized her nomination as an example of nominating an opposition party incumbent lawmaker as minister, which is absurd. Rep. Yong was not elected as a current opposition party candidate. She was elected as a proportional representative of the Together Democratic Alliance, a satellite party of the Democratic Party in 2024, then returned to the Basic Income Party through a "loophole expulsion" procedure. It was precisely because of this that the Basic Income Party retained parliamentary status and now receives government subsidies. Her initial election in 2020 followed the same pattern. Everyone knows this history, yet she claims to have been nominated as an opposition lawmakers representative—is this supposed to be a model case of bipartisan cooperation? She even compared the relationship to the "DJP Alliance" between Kim Dae-jung and Kim Jong-pil, revealing an overestimation of herself that is beyond measure. Rep. Yong should seriously reflect on why even those within the ruling bloc are raising concerns about the inevitability of her resignation, and even her withdrawal. In an era when fairness is valued, can a politician who has benefited from loopholes and tricks truly be considered qualified to serve as a minister of the Republic of Korea?

editorial.title: Paper prosperity
editorial.body: Korea nears $40,000 per capita GNI, but growth is uneven, youth struggle for jobs A nation can cross a $40,000 income threshold without a single dollar reaching the average kitchen table. That uncomfortable contradiction now captures the dilemma at the heart of South Korea’s economy. The Bank of Korea on Tuesday projected that per capita gross national income will exceed $40,000 in 2026, assuming exchange rates hold steady and external shocks stay at bay. After 12 years in the $30,000 range since first crossing that threshold in 2014, the country is finally poised to move up. The milestone is meaningful; however, it is an unusually poor measure of how evenly the economy generates and distributes new income. The latest national accounts explain why. Nominal gross domestic product jumped 26.4 percent from a year earlier in the second quarter, its fastest increase since 1979. Real GNI rose 15.6 percent, the strongest annual gain since 1988. Much of that acceleration, however, comes from a semiconductor boom fueled by global AI investment. In the first eight months, semiconductors accounted for 40.6 percent of exports, with shipments surging 169.6 percent from a year earlier. Such concentration matters because national income is an average. It can rise sharply even when the gains are concentrated in a narrow slice of the economy. The exchange rate adds another layer. Per capita GNI is expressed in dollars, so a stronger won can lift the figure even when productive capacity has changed little. The won’s movement from near 1,600 per dollar to the 1,300s has further inflated the dollar-denominated figure. More important is what happens after corporate profits rise. Chipmakers like Samsung Electronics and SK hynix can earn enormous sums without creating a comparable number of domestic jobs. Gross operating surplus, for instance, rose 18.5 percent in the second quarter from the previous quarter, while employee compensation increased just 1.9 percent. Some gains may reach households through wages, bonuses and dividends, but the path is neither immediate nor assured. Young workers have little reason to celebrate the headline figure. Employment among people aged 15 to 29 fell for the 46th consecutive month in August, declining by 143,000 from a year earlier. Among unemployed young people, 52.7 percent reported experiencing burnout, according to a government survey. Equally problematic is productivity. Korea has become exceptionally good at adding capital to its strongest industries, while productivity gains elsewhere remain modest. A savings rate of 45.6 percent in the second quarter shows that money is hardly scarce. The question is where it goes. Capital needs to flow toward research, new businesses and human capital. Labor markets and education also need to help workers move into areas where demand is growing. Yet workplace-based vocational training accounted for only 1.5 percent of Korea’s training expenditure in 2024, compared with an OECD average of 11.7 percent. The government should treat $40,000 as a checkpoint, not a trophy. Its priority should be raising productivity beyond semiconductors, expanding effective training and reducing the household debt burden that suppresses consumption. Fiscal policy should also avoid stimulating demand in ways that run against monetary restraint. Korea’s journey from a meager $67 in per capita income in 1953 to $40,000 is an undisputed triumph. Yet an economy that depends heavily on capital concentrated in a few industries and favorable valuation effects offers no guarantee of lasting stability. Unless structural reforms broaden the flow of corporate gains to households, raise productivity beyond the leading industries and reconnect young workers with the labor market, $40,000 will stand as a paper victory, reflecting a high-water mark on corporate balance sheets rather than broad-based prosperity. editorial.bodyTr: 한국이 국민 1인당 총국민소득 4만 달러에 근접하고 있지만, 성장이 불균형하고 청년들의 일자리 확보가 어려워지고 있다. 국가가 4만 달러 소득 기준을 넘어설 수 있어도, 평균 가정의 밥상에는 한 푼도 닿지 않을 수 있다. 이 불편한 모순이 지금 한국 경제의 핵심 딜레마를 보여주고 있다. 한국은행이 지난 화요일 2026년 국민 1인당 총국민소득이 4만 달러를 넘을 것으로 전망했는데, 환율이 안정적이고 대외 충격이 없다는 가정 하에서의 예측이다. 2014년 처음 3만 달러 기준을 넘은 이후 12년간 3만 달러대에 머물러 있던 한국이 드디어 한 단계 올라설 준비를 하고 있는 것이다. 이 마지노선은 의미가 있지만, 경제가 얼마나 고르게 새로운 소득을 창출하고 분배하는지를 측정하는 척도로는 놀랍도록 부족하다. 최근 국민계정이 그 이유를 잘 설명한다. 명목 국내총생산이 2분기에 전년 대비 26.4% 급증해 1979년 이후 가장 빠른 증가율을 기록했다. 실질 총국민소득은 15.6% 상승해 1988년 이후 가장 큰 연간 증가폭을 보였다. 하지만 이러한 가속도의 대부분은 글로벌 인공지능 투자로 촉발된 반도체 호황에서 비롯된 것이다. 처음 8개월 동안 반도체가 수출의 40.6%를 차지했으며, 선적량이 전년 대비 169.6% 급증했다. 이러한 집중도가 중요한 이유는 국민소득이 평균이기 때문이다. 경제의 극히 일부에만 이득이 집중되어 있어도 평균은 급격히 상승할 수 있다. 환율이 또 다른 변수를 더한다. 국민 1인당 총국민소득은 달러로 표시되므로, 원화 강세는 생산 능력의 변화가 거의 없어도 그 수치를 높일 수 있다. 달러당 1,600원대에서 1,300원대로의 원화 상승이 달러 표시 수치를 더욱 부풀렸다. 더 중요한 것은 기업 이익 증가 이후에 어떤 일이 벌어지느냐 하는 것이다. 삼성전자나 SK하이닉스 같은 칩 제조업체들은 국내 일자리를 크게 늘리지 않으면서도 막대한 이익을 올릴 수 있다. 예를 들어 총 영업 잉여는 2분기에 전분기 대비 18.5% 증가했지만, 근로자 보수는 단 1.9%만 증가했다. 일부 이득이 임금, 보너스, 배당금을 통해 가정에 도달할 수 있지만, 그 경로는 즉시적이지도 않고 보장되지도 않는다. 청년 근로자들이 이 헤드라인 수치를 축하할 이유는 거의 없다. 15~29세 인구의 고용이 8월에 46개월 연속 감소했으며, 전년 대비 14만 3천 명이 줄었다. 실직 상태의 청년 중 52.7%가 정부 조사에서 번아웃을 경험했다고 보고했다. 똑같이 문제가 되는 것은 생산성이다. 한국은 가장 강한 산업에 자본을 추가하는 것은 예외적으로 잘하지만, 다른 분야의 생산성 향상은 미미하다. 2분기 저축률 45.6%는 돈이 부족하지 않다는 것을 보여준다. 문제는 그 돈이 어디로 가느냐이다. 자본은 연구, 새로운 사업, 인적 자본으로 흘러야 한다. 노동 시장과 교육도 수요가 증가하는 분야로 근로자들이 이동하도록 도와야 한다. 그런데 직장 기반 직업 훈련이 2024년 한국의 훈련 지출에서 차지하는 비중은 1.5%에 불과한 반면, 경제협력개발기구(OECD) 평균은 11.7%이다. 정부는 4만 달러를 트로피가 아니라 중간 지점으로 봐야 한다. 정부의 우선순위는 반도체를 넘어선 생산성 향상, 효과적인 훈련 확대, 소비를 억압하는 가계 부채 부담 감소여야 한다. 재정 정책은 또한 금리 억제에 반대되는 방식으로 수요를 자극하는 것을 피해야 한다. 한국이 1953년 국민 1인당 67달러에서 4만 달러로 나아간 여정은 의심할 여지 없는 승리이다. 하지만 소수 산업에 집중된 자본에 크게 의존하고 호의적인 평가 효과에 의존하는 경제는 지속적인 안정을 보장하지 않는다. 구조적 개혁을 통해 기업 이익의 흐름을 가정으로 확대하고, 주도 산업을 넘어선 생산성을 높이고, 청년 근로자들을 노동 시장과 다시 연결하지 않는 한, 4만 달러는 기업 재무제표의 고점을 반영하는 종잇장 같은 승리로 남을 것이며, 광범위한 번영과는 거리가 멀 것이다.

editorials.title: Paper prosperity
editorials.body: Korea nears $40,000 per capita GNI, but growth is uneven, youth struggle for jobs A nation can cross a $40,000 income threshold without a single dollar reaching the average kitchen table. That uncomfortable contradiction now captures the dilemma at the heart of South Korea’s economy. The Bank of Korea on Tuesday projected that per capita gross national income will exceed $40,000 in 2026, assuming exchange rates hold steady and external shocks stay at bay. After 12 years in the $30,000 range since first crossing that threshold in 2014, the country is finally poised to move up. The milestone is meaningful; however, it is an unusually poor measure of how evenly the economy generates and distributes new income. The latest national accounts explain why. Nominal gross domestic product jumped 26.4 percent from a year earlier in the second quarter, its fastest increase since 1979. Real GNI rose 15.6 percent, the strongest annual gain since 1988. Much of that acceleration, however, comes from a semiconductor boom fueled by global AI investment. In the first eight months, semiconductors accounted for 40.6 percent of exports, with shipments surging 169.6 percent from a year earlier. Such concentration matters because national income is an average. It can rise sharply even when the gains are concentrated in a narrow slice of the economy. The exchange rate adds another layer. Per capita GNI is expressed in dollars, so a stronger won can lift the figure even when productive capacity has changed little. The won’s movement from near 1,600 per dollar to the 1,300s has further inflated the dollar-denominated figure. More important is what happens after corporate profits rise. Chipmakers like Samsung Electronics and SK hynix can earn enormous sums without creating a comparable number of domestic jobs. Gross operating surplus, for instance, rose 18.5 percent in the second quarter from the previous quarter, while employee compensation increased just 1.9 percent. Some gains may reach households through wages, bonuses and dividends, but the path is neither immediate nor assured. Young workers have little reason to celebrate the headline figure. Employment among people aged 15 to 29 fell for the 46th consecutive month in August, declining by 143,000 from a year earlier. Among unemployed young people, 52.7 percent reported experiencing burnout, according to a government survey. Equally problematic is productivity. Korea has become exceptionally good at adding capital to its strongest industries, while productivity gains elsewhere remain modest. A savings rate of 45.6 percent in the second quarter shows that money is hardly scarce. The question is where it goes. Capital needs to flow toward research, new businesses and human capital. Labor markets and education also need to help workers move into areas where demand is growing. Yet workplace-based vocational training accounted for only 1.5 percent of Korea’s training expenditure in 2024, compared with an OECD average of 11.7 percent. The government should treat $40,000 as a checkpoint, not a trophy. Its priority should be raising productivity beyond semiconductors, expanding effective training and reducing the household debt burden that suppresses consumption. Fiscal policy should also avoid stimulating demand in ways that run against monetary restraint. Korea’s journey from a meager $67 in per capita income in 1953 to $40,000 is an undisputed triumph. Yet an economy that depends heavily on capital concentrated in a few industries and favorable valuation effects offers no guarantee of lasting stability. Unless structural reforms broaden the flow of corporate gains to households, raise productivity beyond the leading industries and reconnect young workers with the labor market, $40,000 will stand as a paper victory, reflecting a high-water mark on corporate balance sheets rather than broad-based prosperity. The government must manage fund operation principles more rigorously.
Maximizing the substantive effectiveness of the fund requires enhanced transparency and accountability.
